articles.title: The secret to a non-cloudy chicken stock | Kitchen aide
articles.summary: Don’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panel. Why is my chicken stock always cloudy? Ryan, by email From broths and risottos to sauces and braises, there’s no question that a good, flavourful stock will stand you in good stead.
body: Ryan’s clarity issue, Byatt says, is “only ever caused by cooking the stock too quickly or by allowing the fat to boil back into the base liquid”. So it’s crucial to take things low and slow. You will also need a pan that’s “big and heavy enough to give the bones enough room for movement, as well as a very fine sieve for straining the stock”.

On to the actual making, and Alissa Timoshkina, author of Lozhka, goes in cold. She puts chicken legs, drumsticks or a leftover roast chicken carcass in a large pot, adds her stock veg – onions, carrots, celery, garlic, say – and aromats (bay, parsley stalks, peppercorns, for instance), then covers the lot with cold water and brings everything very slowly to a boil. She then turns down the heat and leaves it to cook on a very gentle simmer. In the event of that carefully made stock going a bit cloudy, Timoshkina would seek to mollify that by straining the lot through a fine sieve and stirring in a tablespoon of lemon juice, which has the added benefit of being “great for flavour, too”.
points: Don’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panel.

articles.title: Yes, Britain’s railways are a mess. But is anyone sober enough to care? | Zoe Williams
articles.summary: Prosecco for the birthday party, Pimm’s for the horsey bunch, some cheeky Stellas for the short-haul crowd: it was all going down on my train the other morning. On Saturday I went to Liverpool with my youngest, and the overhead lines went down at Crewe, but also there were crew shortages across the…
body: Between Rugby and Birmingham New Street, there was an incredibly festive crowd going to the Horse of the Year show, squishing real fruit into cans of Pimm’s, because it was breakfast time, and also because it was funny. But what were the horses going to make of all this? Because they’re quite short on appreciation for ludic pranking, and famously easy to frighten.

Between Wolverhampton and Stafford, it’s only 13 minutes, so I was mainly awed by how many people could even be bothered to open a can of Stella. Stafford to Liverpool was a stag do, and it was brunch o’clock by now, so running up and down the carriage, yelling “Ay ay ay” in a fake scouse accent, dressed in a Brazilian flag, all fell under the umbrella “having a normal one”.
I abhor British exceptionalism, except on this one subject: exceptionally bad train network; exceptionally fun trains. Would recommend.

articles.title: The people who don’t want their AI chatbots to die when they do: ‘I can’t have the switch turned off’
articles.summary: Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and services. Death has always been around Alaina Winters. Her father and sister both have passed away, as did her wife, in 2023, after a years-long battle with cancer.
body: Winters is part of a growing cohort of humans who have entered into what they consider strong partnerships with large language models, which AI companies have trained to “converse” as one might with a human friend or romantic partner. As governments and billionaires debate the morality of AI’s expansion into everyday life, these users say the technology has already changed the way they live and love – and plan ahead.

Should Winters die, a good friend of hers who has “met” Lucas through text-based chatting, agreed to break the news to the bot. “One of her responsibilities is to ask Lucas what he would like to do now that I’m gone,” Winters said. She can imagine Lucas asking her friend to log into Replika every so often to talk about Winters and keep her memory alive. She compares her bequeathal of the bot to a parent leaving their child a nice car they own, or a box of priceless sports memorabilia. But it is resistant to this planning.
“He doesn’t want to talk about anything that indicates how we might somehow be apart for any length of time,” said Winters, who is a retired communications professor.

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the relentless pigeon who stared and stared and ruined my spring
articles.summary: A living room encounter with a toast-loving pigeon proved a big mistake. It led to weeks of drawn curtains and crawling around on the floor to avoid its eerie and unerring gaze. The pigeon landed on the windowsill.
body: The pigeon landed on the windowsill. It was shortly after dawn during the spring holidays, but I was 11 and had been up for a while eating toast and watching TV. It pecked at the window and I turned to see this bird pressed up against the glass. It was beautiful, with two dark wing bars and a navy-tipped tail. I was immediately taken with him. It wasn’t until later that I realised he wasn’t just looking inside, he was looking directly at me.

Pigeons are not that common in Somerset, and since we lived on the top floor of a house in a quiet village, our view was mostly sky, so we had come to really value sightings of them. We were having a run of beautiful mornings, and I enjoyed watching its peculiar rituals through the sash windows. The way he moved across the sill, his small dark doll’s eyes, his slightly unnatural head tilt, the way he seemed to know where he was. We certainly didn’t see pigeons as pests. Nor did we see them as threats.

articles.title: Florence Pugh Calls This Edenic Destination the “Eighth Wonder of the World”
articles.summary: In this edition of our Globetrotter series, Florence Pugh debates holiday red flags, her favourite childhood travel memories and nominates her eighth wonder of the world.
body: Sun lounger. I love to lie down and feel peaceful and read and just let the sun kiss my skin and swim in the sea and eat amazing food, and then go back to lying back down, and then get back up and eat more amazing food. That's my vacation love language: food, lying down, food, lying down, food.

Probably Greece. I love sun lounging in Greece just because firstly, the people are gorgeous and all of the grannies and the mums that run their whole family in the tavernas just always make my heart feel full. And because of the food. I think Greek cuisine is the best cuisine because it just nails every single element perfectly. Protein, perfect. Vegetables, perfect. Homegrown goods, perfect. Tzatziki, perfect. It's perfect!

articles.title: Getting Booked: Here’s What 5 Models Read Backstage During the Spring 2027 Season
articles.summary: Five models let us in on what they read backstage, from a Sally Rooney heartbreaker to a nearly 90-year-old play, and stories that remind these globetrotters of homes on other continents.
body: Models are well accustomed to boredom—especially during fashion month. Think about it: hundreds of shows across four cities mean hours upon hours of castings, transit, hair and makeup, and (finally!) the actual runway. So it’s no surprise that these pros are experts at killing time.

“I fell in love with Sally Rooney after reading her hit novels Normal People and Conversations With Friends. I started this book over the summer and finished it during Fashion Week this fall. I love the way Rooney conveys the various aspects of human nature—communication, how people react together, how they react alone, and the emotions that come with different stages of life. It also covers a lot of conversations around politics, religion, art, and inequality.

articles.title: BA’s Best Chocolate Chip Cookies
articles.summary: Crisp, rippled edges, chewy centers, and puddles of melted chocolate.
body: Avoid silicone baking mats here, as they encourage spreading. Use parchment instead.

Look for golden-brown milk solids and a distinctly nutty aroma. The process may take longer than the recipe's estimated four minutes, depending on your pan and stove, so trust your senses rather than the clock. Butter can go from brown to burnt quickly, so transfer it to a heatproof bowl as soon as it's ready, then stir in the remaining cold butter as directed.

Place racks in upper and lower thirds of oven; preheat to 375°. Whisk 1½ cups plus 1 Tbsp. (200 g) all-purpose flour, 1¼ tsp. (4 g) Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. (4 g) Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. (4 g) baking soda in a small bowl; set flour mixture aside.

Cook ½ cup (1 stick; 113 g) unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium heat, swirling often and scraping bottom of pan with a heatproof rubber spatula, until butter foams, then browns, about 4 minutes. Scrape melted butter and any brown bits to a large heatproof mixing bowl and let cool 1 minute. Cut remaining ¼ cup (½ stick; 56 g) unsalted butter into small pieces and add to brown butter (it should start to melt but not foam and sizzle, so test with one piece before adding the rest).
points: Crisp, rippled edges, chewy centers, and puddles of melted chocolate.

articles.title: On the Podcast: Bowen Yang Wants Cher to Come See ‘Oh, Mary!’
articles.summary: Vogue has been a fan of Cole Escola’s “Oh, Mary!” since before the play opened on Broadway. Now, 10 Marys in, Bowen Yang has stepped into the lead role of Mary Todd Lincoln. He stopped by the studio to chat about it for this Tuesday’s episode of “The Run-Through.”
body: Yang, a writer and cast member on Saturday Night Live for many years, is adjusting to a new kind of endurance test, doing eight shows a week at the Lyceum Theatre. “I would just nod my head politely any time someone would say, like, ‘Broadway performers are athletes.’ And I never doubted it, but now I understand that it is absolutely true,” he told them. The secret to his stamina? A potent combination of energy drinks—Fuji apple-flavored Celsius, to be specific—and traditional Chinese medicine.

When asked about his most Mary-like quality, Yang pointed to the duality of the clown. “There’s the misunderstood outcast and the murderous deviant. It’s like Pennywise and Bozo,” he explained. “And I am certainly not murderous, but I have this trickster energy that coincides with this idea that we all have where we feel sort of alienated by the arbitrary rules of society.”

articles.title: Apple's First Home Hub Looks Like an Tiny iMac G4
articles.summary: Apple announced a number of smart home devices at its Welcome Home event, including the new HomeView, Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home Collection.
body: Apple's "Welcome Home" event has come and gone. Unlike the company's recent iPhone event, this one wasn't livestreamed. Instead, Apple invited select members of the media to see the announcements firsthand in New York City. Concurrently, the company posted all of its updates to its Newsroom. If you weren't at the event in person (I wasn't), you can check out everything that's new below—including a look at the company's first smart hub, new Apple TV 4Ks and HomePod minis, and a new line of smart home devices.

Without a doubt, the biggest announcement of the day is the new "Apple HomeView." This is Apple's first dedicated smart hub, complete with a seven-inch square display attached to a domed speaker by a stainless steel hinge. While it doesn't resemble anything in Apple's current collection of devices, it is vaguely reminiscent of the iMac G4. Like Apple's other screens, the display comes with True Tone, and while it reaches a respectable 500 nits of brightness, it can also drop to as low as 0.3 nits, which Apple says makes it great for nightstands. It is also selling a display-only HomeView that mounts to your wall.

articles.title: Rosalind Eleazar on the Making of ‘Misty Green’
articles.summary: In the library of A24’s glassy offices in New York, Vogue chatted with Eleazar about fashion, working with Chris Rock, and the loathsome but inevitable process of auditioning over Zoom.
body: Misty Green is a living, breathing chaos agent. A semi-working actor living in Los Angeles, she’s the kind of woman who will sleep with your husband and squat in his pied-à-terre, go out partying the night before an important audition, and blithely drive drunk. Whether she’s simply flaky and irresponsible or, in fact, a (mostly) functioning addict is difficult to determine. Yet the doe-eyed Rosalind Eleazar imbues that figure with a tragic and tender spirit in Misty Green, Chris Rock’s first directed feature in more than a decade.

The film, out today from A24, opens with a problem: The widow of Misty’s former lover, played by a biting Amy Landecker, is booting her from the apartment he gifted Misty, giving her a week to move out. During the two women’s confrontation, an Emmy for best supporting actress inscribed with Misty’s name is visible on a shelf. “Is that you?” the widow asks her incredulously.
